The UN only gained oversight of ICANN, the organization that allocates large IP address blocks and manages TLDs registrations. The internet has not been "handed over to the UN." Anyone claiming so is misinformed or being misleading.

If ICANN nullified all of .com tomorrow you (or your ISP, or their ISP) could, in 5 minutes, switch to an alternate DNS root server and continue happily accessing websites under .com domains. IP block allocations are a little more complicated but my understanding is that a top level ISP (backbone) is still voluntarily obeying ICANN's allocations and could simply continue using the IPs that ICANN revoked.

Bottom line: ICANN have no power to block anything. They exist so that 2 people can't claim the same domain or IP address. Obeying their allocations is voluntary.
